Consider the following game (called To court the king, thanks to @Joachim Breitner for telling me about it): You toss nnn coins, each of which comes up head with probability p∈(0,1)p \in (0,1)p∈(0,1). You need to set aside at least one of them, which will not be tossed again, and you toss the remaining coins. This continues (for at most nnn rounds, apparently) until all coins have been set aside. Your goal is to maximize the probability that all coins end up head. 

Inspired by recent developments, I started some vibe-proving sessions trying to find the best strategy in this game depending on ppp. (Some three years ago, I could only solve the case p>1/2p>1/2p>1/2 on paper, but got stuck on p<1/2p<1/2p<1/2.) Claude made some mistakes but finally came up with a proof for p=1/2−δp = 1/2 - \deltap=1/2−δ for δ>0\delta>0δ>0 small enough. Since my trust was not too high, I asked Claude for a formalization of his proof in Lean (I knew that all foundations are in mathlib), and it came through. (There is only one definition needed for the theorem, which I carefully checked. The Lean code will not PRed to Mathlib, since it only treats that special game.) 

Today, I sent the corresponding manuscript (after carefully checking everything as usual) off to a probability journal, since the mathematical novelty is rather the result on the probabilistic game than its formalization. (Of course, including all details of the use of generative AI, including history of prompts.) Really curious what will happen...

Is there any experience from other fields of mathematics how journals have treated such (much help from AI, but formalized) submissions? I'd like to share my experience.

All details, in particular the manuscript are in the github repo.

I'm about to submit an "experiment" of my own. Essentially, it's a "classic" number theory paper, where most lemmas and theorems have a link to the Lean code in the GitHub repo. I'm also quite unsure how this will be received... I don't mean to hijack your thread @Peter Pfaffelhuber, but I'm very interested to see how this trend will develop. And if you find a venue (outside of this Zulip) where this particular topic is being discussed, I'd be grateful if you'd let me know.

Thanks for sharing, @Fernando Portela, I think we have the same feelings about our contributions! However, if papers such as ours have a chance to be published, this is a great opportunity for all people working in formalizing mathematics.
@Peter Pfaffelhuber Did you consider using Comparator to verify the proof? Maybe a structure similar to https://github.com/frenzymath/Anderson-Conjecture with a Challenge.lean file?

Thanks for bringing comparator to my attention. This is exactly the tool I wanted to have in the first place. (I added a Summary.lean file which only consists of the definitions and the result, with the intent that a reader/referee only has to check that file.) I asked Claude to run comparator (of course, carefully checking the Challenge.lean file.) The outcome Your solution is okay! tells me that everything is fine.

Side note for running comparator: First I got an uncaught exception: Const does not match between challenge and target 'w' (where w is the recursively defined function I use in the main result. Claude tells me this is because the definition uses termination_by and decreasing_by which apparently can end up differently after elaboration. Hope the solution (making a file with definitions, which is imported by both, Challenge.lean as well as the solution, is ok.)

Claude suggestion for Const does not match between challenge and target

This is the elaboration-mismatch problem I half-anticipated. Both Challenge.lean and CoinsLean.Optimal.lean declare w from byte-identical source, but Lean's elaborator produces slightly different kernel terms when compiling the two files independently — w's body contains a by block (the membership proof for attach.sup''s non-empty witness) plus a  termination_by/decreasing_by block, both of which can elaborate to non-identical proof terms across two compilation runs even with the same source.
Anderson's Challenge.lean got away with re-declaration because their definitions are pure def := <expr> with no embedded tactics. Ours aren't. The fix is to put the definitions in a single shared module that both Challenge.lean and the existing CoinsLean modules import. Then there's only one kernel definition of w, and the comparator has nothing to disagree about. Let me check the comparator behaviour to confirm my diagnosis before refactoring.

Peter Pfaffelhuber schrieb:

. Hope the solution (making a file with definitions, which is imported by both, Challenge.lean as well as the solution, is ok.)

Yes, absolutely fine!
